title: What is a partial index (indexing only rows matching a condition, e.g. `WHERE deleted = false`), and when is it worth it?
shortTitle: What is a partial index, and when is it worth it

s1_definition.profdef: A partial index (called a filtered index in SQL Server) is an index built over only the subset of rows that satisfy a predicate, specified with a `WHERE` clause on the index definition. Because it indexes fewer rows, it is smaller, faster to scan, and cheaper to maintain, and it is used by the optimizer only for queries whose predicate is implied by the index's filter. It is worth it when queries consistently target a small, well-defined slice of a large table, such as active rows, pending rows, or non-deleted rows.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, imagine ninety-nine percent of loan applications are already CLOSED and only a tiny fraction are PENDING review. A full index on status would waste space indexing millions of closed loans that nobody searches for. A partial index is like keeping a small, separate tray on the officer's desk holding only the pending applications. It is tiny, instantly scannable, and exactly matches what the officer actually looks for all day. You do not index the giant pile of closed loans at all, because no query ever hunts through them.
s1_definition.oneliner: A partial index covers only the rows matching a condition, so it is small and fast — worth it when your queries always target a small slice of a big table.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A partial index (called a filtered index in SQL Server) is an index built over only the subset of rows that satisfy a predicate, specified with a `WHERE` clause on the index definition. Because it indexes fewer rows, it is smaller, faster to scan, and cheaper to maintain, and it is used by the optimizer only for queries whose predicate is implied by the index's filter. It is worth it when queries consistently target a small, well-defined slice of a large table, such as active rows, pending rows, or non-deleted rows.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, imagine ninety-nine percent of loan applications are already CLOSED and only a tiny fraction are PENDING review. A full index on status would waste space indexing millions of closed loans that nobody searches for. A partial index is like keeping a small, separate tray on the officer's desk holding only the pending applications. It is tiny, instantly scannable, and exactly matches what the officer actually looks for all day. You do not index the giant pile of closed loans at all, because no query ever hunts through them.

**One line to remember:** A partial index covers only the rows matching a condition, so it is small and fast — worth it when your queries always target a small slice of a big table.

sections.s2_technical:
A partial index is defined with a predicate, for example `CREATE INDEX ix_pending ON loans(applied_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING'`. The index stores entries only for rows where status is PENDING. All the CLOSED rows are simply not in the index, so it stays tiny no matter how large the table grows.

The optimizer uses a partial index only when it can prove the query's predicate is a subset of the index's filter. A query `WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND applied_at < ?` matches, because the planner knows every qualifying row is in the partial index. A query without the `status = 'PENDING'` condition cannot use it, because rows outside the filter are absent.

The benefits are threefold. Size: a partial index on one percent of rows is roughly one percent of the size of a full index, so it fits in memory and scans faster. Write cost: inserts and updates only touch the index when the row matches the filter, so the ninety-nine percent of writes that are CLOSED loans never pay to maintain this index. Selectivity: it sidesteps the low-selectivity problem — a full index on a status column where almost everything is CLOSED is nearly useless, but a partial index on the rare PENDING value is highly effective.

Partial indexes also enforce conditional uniqueness elegantly. You can write a unique partial index like `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_one_primary ON accounts(customer_id) WHERE is_primary = true`, which guarantees each customer has at most one primary account while allowing many non-primary ones. A senior nuance: in PostgreSQL the query predicate must be clearly implied by the index predicate for the planner to use it, so vague or dynamic predicates can silently miss the index; and immutable boolean or enum filters work best. Another nuance is that partial indexes are perfect for soft-delete patterns — `WHERE deleted = false` — so queries over live data stay fast while deleted rows never bloat the index.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The loan review dashboard only ever lists PENDING loans, yet the loans table holds tens of millions of mostly CLOSED loans. A full status index is huge and barely selective. This is exactly the case for a partial index on PENDING rows only.

Problem 2 — The accounts table uses soft deletes with a `deleted` flag, and every live query filters `deleted = false`. Indexing deleted rows wastes space. This is exactly the soft-delete partial index.

Problem 3 — Each customer may have many accounts but at most one marked primary. This is exactly a unique partial index enforcing conditional uniqueness.

The mini-project builds a loan-review service backed by a partial index on pending loans, plus a partial unique index guaranteeing one primary account per customer, and shows the optimizer using the small partial index.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/partial-index-service-1.0.0.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev

# Query matching the partial predicate → uses the small ix_pending_loans
psql -d bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM loans
  WHERE status='PENDING' AND applied_at < NOW() ORDER BY applied_at;"
# Expect: Index Scan using ix_pending_loans

# Partial unique index enforces one primary account per customer
psql -d bankdb -c "INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('A1','CUST1',true);"
psql -d bankdb -c "INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('A2','CUST1',true);"
# Expect: second insert fails — duplicate key violates ux_one_primary
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the loan dashboard requests all PENDING loans older than today for review, from a table of tens of millions of mostly CLOSED loans.

Step 1 — The service calls `pendingOlderThan(now)`, producing a query whose predicate includes `status = 'PENDING'` and a range on applied-at.

Step 2 — The planner checks the partial index `ix_pending_loans`, whose filter is `status = 'PENDING'`. Because the query's predicate includes exactly that condition, the planner proves every qualifying row is in the partial index and chooses it.

Step 3 — The partial index is tiny, holding only the handful of pending loans, not the millions of closed ones. The engine seeks into it and walks the applied-at order, returning LN001 and skipping the CLOSED LN002, which is not even present in the index.

Step 4 — Separately, when a new CLOSED loan is inserted, this partial index is not touched at all, because the row does not match the filter, so the write pays nothing to maintain it.

Step 5 — For the accounts side, inserting a second primary account for the same customer is rejected by the partial unique index, which enforces at most one primary per customer while allowing many non-primary accounts.

```text
2026-10-25 15:31:11 INFO  LoanReviewService - Listing PENDING loans older than 2026-10-25T15:31 via tiny partial index ix_pending_loans
2026-10-25 15:31:11 INFO  LoanReviewService - Live (not deleted) loans for SAV2001 via partial index ix_live_loans
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  loans table: 10M CLOSED + 50 PENDING
    │
    ▼
  ix_pending_loans  (WHERE status='PENDING')  ← indexes only 50 rows
    │
  Query: WHERE status='PENDING' AND applied_at < now
    │ predicate ⊆ index filter → planner uses partial index
    ▼
  seek 50-row index → walk applied_at → LN001 (CLOSED LN002 absent)
    │
    ▼
  pending loans for review

  INSERT CLOSED loan → does NOT match filter → partial index untouched (free write)
  INSERT 2nd primary account (CUST1) → ux_one_primary → REJECTED
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A partial index, which SQL Server calls a filtered index, is an index built over only the rows that satisfy a predicate, written as a WHERE clause on the index itself. Because it indexes a subset rather than the whole table, it is dramatically smaller, faster to scan, and cheaper to maintain, and the optimizer uses it only for queries whose predicate is implied by the index's filter. It is worth it exactly when your queries consistently target a small, well-defined slice of a large table — active rows, pending rows, or non-deleted rows.

The benefits are threefold. First, size: a partial index over one percent of rows is roughly one percent of the size of a full index, so it stays in memory and scans quickly. Second, write cost: inserts and updates only maintain the index when the row matches the filter, so the vast majority of writes that fall outside the filter pay nothing. Third, selectivity: it neatly solves the low-selectivity problem, because a full index on a status column where almost everything is closed is nearly useless, whereas a partial index on the rare pending value is highly effective. As a bonus, a unique partial index enforces conditional uniqueness, like at most one primary account per customer.

At the National Bank of India our loan-review dashboard only ever listed pending loans, but the loans table held tens of millions of mostly closed ones. A full status index was huge and barely selective, so I built a partial index on applied-at with the filter status equals pending. It indexed only the few dozen pending loans, the dashboard became instant, and the millions of closed-loan writes stopped paying to maintain it. I also used a partial unique index on the primary-account flag to guarantee each customer had at most one primary account while allowing many ordinary ones.

The nuance I always raise is that in PostgreSQL the query's predicate must be clearly implied by the index's filter for the planner to use the partial index, so I keep the filter on immutable boolean or enum columns and I confirm with EXPLAIN that the small partial index is actually chosen rather than a full scan.

Covering index: all query columns in index — no table lookup needed
